analysis.title: Gridlock and diplomatic hopes lift US stocks (UBS House View - CIO Alert)
key_insights: S&P 500 closed +1.6% on Wednesday, reversing the initial negative futures reaction to Democrats winning both the House and the Senate. Nasdaq Composite rose 1.4%.
The 10-year US Treasury yield fell 8bps from its level before the election result. DXY dollar index fell 0.3%.

Brent crude fell 8.2% to around USD 95/bbl on position squaring and hopes for US-Iran diplomacy. Qatar has stepped up mediation, but Iranian officials said a deal is only possible if the US accepts Iran's seven points.
With Democrats controlling Congress and Trump holding the presidency and veto, abrupt tax and spending changes should be harder. UBS says the election removed a source of uncertainty.
The S&P 500 gained an average of 15.5% in the six months after the previous 14 midterm elections since 1970. UBS says this is not a forecast and may reflect the removal of election uncertainty.

Remaining political risks: the next Congress must address government funding and the debt ceiling, which could raise bond market volatility. Trump keeps broad executive authority over tariffs, foreign policy and regulation.

Democratic gains in data-center states such as Texas and Georgia could delay projects, raise costs or shift where capacity is built. Large technology platforms rose Wednesday while some data-center construction names fell on concern over scrutiny of electricity use, water use and permitting.

Investors favor financially strong platforms that can fund investment from existing cash flow over businesses exposed to financing, construction, permitting or execution risk. UBS expects broad equity gains with greater dispersion within technology.
UBS keeps growth, earnings, inflation and interest rates as the primary market drivers. Recent corporate results show robust demand across parts of technology and the broader economy.

Oil: global inventories have fallen sharply and pledged strategic reserve releases are largely complete. Record freight costs, constrained tanker capacity and recovering Chinese imports are likely to keep prices elevated. Trump's comment that no military strike is imminent weighed on prices, and it is unclear how long the US will keep military escorts for energy flows.
Positioning: stay invested in diversified equities. Preferred sectors are industrials, health care and financials. Preferred regions are the Eurozone, emerging markets and Asia ex-Japan.
UBS advises rebalancing concentrated technology positions into strength and diversifying across the AI value chain, favoring financially strong platforms and high-quality infrastructure providers.
UBS advises keeping protection against geopolitical disruption through broad commodity exposure across energy, precious metals, industrial metals and agriculture.

sector_views.rationale: Named as a preferred sector alongside strong earnings and resilient growth.

Constructive on AI infrastructure demand, but advises trimming concentrated positions. Expects greater dispersion, with data-center scrutiny and AI monetization questions raising single-stock volatility.

earnings_insights: UBS says recent corporate results provide further evidence of robust demand across parts of the technology sector and the broader economy. The note gives no company-specific EPS or revenue figures.

risk_factors: Government funding and debt ceiling negotiations in the next Congress could raise bond market volatility.
Democratic gains in data-center states could delay projects, raise development costs or change where capacity is built.
Trump retains broad executive authority over tariffs, foreign policy and regulation.
A breakdown in US-Iran negotiations or renewed attacks could push oil prices higher.
Continued undersupply could further deplete commercial oil stocks, with record freight costs and constrained tanker capacity.
Uncertainty over how long the US will support energy flows with military escorts.
Questions over AI monetization alongside data-center scrutiny could increase single-stock volatility.
vol_and_positioning: UBS expects the uneven rally to bring greater dispersion in technology-sector performance and higher single-stock volatility from data-center scrutiny and AI monetization questions.
Upcoming government funding and debt ceiling negotiations could increase bond market volatility.
Brent's 8.2% drop partly reflects position squaring.
UBS recommends rebalancing concentrated single-stock technology exposure and keeping broad commodity exposure as a hedge against geopolitical disruption.
geopolitical: US-Iran conflict: Qatar has stepped up mediation as Washington and Tehran appear to seek to resume talks. Iranian officials said an agreement requires the US to accept Iran's seven points.
Trump said no military strike is imminent. The risk of renewed military action remains, and it is an open question how long the US will provide military escorts for energy flows.
US midterm elections: Democrats won both the House and the Senate, with Trump keeping the presidency and veto power.
Energy supply: global inventories have fallen sharply, strategic reserve releases are largely complete, freight costs are at record levels and tanker capacity is constrained.

tension_points.bull_case: Gridlock removes election uncertainty and limits abrupt tax and spending changes. The S&P 500 averaged +15.5% in the six months after the previous 14 midterms, and earnings and AI infrastructure demand remain strong.
tension_points.bear_case: Funding and debt ceiling fights could raise bond volatility, data-center scrutiny could hit capacity-dependent names, and Trump retains tariff and regulatory authority.

tension_points.bull_case: Qatar's mediation and both sides' incentives to avoid a prolonged conflict could lower energy prices further.
tension_points.bear_case: Iran says a deal requires the US to accept its seven points. Inventories are low, strategic reserve releases are largely complete, and freight costs are at records, which keeps prices elevated and exposes markets to renewed attacks.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A breakdown in negotiations or renewed attacks could trigger another rise in oil prices.
